explanation: He held the debates in a House of Worship at Fatehpur Sikri, his new capital. He had books read aloud to him daily and built a huge library.

claims.text: The Mughal emperor Akbar held religious debates among Muslims, Hindus, Christians, Jains, Zoroastrians and others in the Ibadat Khana at Fatehpur Sikri.
Babur founded the Mughal Empire, Jahangir was Akbar's son and successor, and Aurangzeb ruled later and did not host such debates.
Fatehpur Sikri was Akbar's new capital city.
Akbar had books read aloud to him every day and assembled a large library.

claimResults.note: Mainstream view, from Abu'l-Fazl and the Jesuit visitors through modern textbooks. Some scholars suspect the 'unlettered' image was partly cultivated, which is why this is flagged.

issues.note: 'Illiterate' in the stem is the mainstream account, but it adds a contestable detail to an item that Akbar's interfaith debates already pin down. Dropping the word would remove the only soft spot; keeping it is defensible.

editor.reason: Both checks pass on certain knowledge, and every claim is standard risk. B's note on 'illiterate' is fair, but it is the mainstream account and it also separates Akbar from Jahangir, who was literate (B's rival test), so the stem stays.
